title: The Crack in Euclid's First Proof
audience: A curious adult with no background in this field

source.title: Proposition 1
source.authors: Euclid (with an uncredited modern guide and commentary)

intro.summary: The first proposition of Euclid's Elements asks how to build an equilateral triangle, one with three equal sides, on a given line segment AB. Euclid draws two circles of radius AB, one centred at A and one at B, and joins their crossing point C to A and B. He then argues that all three sides are equal. The accompanying commentary shows that this short, clear proof has logical gaps. Nothing in Euclid's stated assumptions guarantees that the circles cross. Nothing rules out the sides overlapping before they reach C. Nothing shows the figure lies flat in a plane. The commentary is a critique of reasoning, not an experiment. Its claims are about what follows from Euclid's stated assumptions, not about whether the triangle exists in ordinary drawings.
background: Euclid's Elements, written in ancient Greece around 300 BCE, built geometry by proving each result from a short list of starting assumptions.
Postulates are assumptions about what you may construct, such as drawing a circle with any centre and radius. Definitions fix what words mean.
Common notions are general rules of reasoning, such as 'things equal to the same thing are equal to each other'.
A proof is only airtight if every step is justified by those stated assumptions or by results already proved.
intro.aha: The very first proof in Euclid's Elements, famous for its clarity, quietly assumes that its two circles cross, and nothing in Euclid's own rules guarantees that they do.

primer.heading: The question
primer.body: You are given one straight line segment, AB. Can you build a triangle on it with all three sides equal, using only a straightedge and compass? This is the very first proposition in Euclid's Elements, the most influential mathematics book ever written.
primer.quote: To construct an equilateral triangle on a given finite straight line.

primer.heading: What Euclid did
primer.body: Draw a circle centred at A that passes through B. Draw a second circle centred at B that passes through A. Where the circles cross, call the point C, and join C to A and to B. Every point on the first circle is as far from A as B is, so AC equals AB. In the same way, BC equals BA. Things equal to the same thing are equal to each other, so all three sides match.
primer.quote: Describe the circle BCD with center A and radius AB. Again describe the circle ACE with center B and radius BA.

primer.heading: What the commentary found
primer.body: The proof looks perfect, yet it relies on facts Euclid never stated. None of his postulates says that the two circles actually cross, so the point C is simply assumed to exist. An ancient critic, Zeno of Sidon, also noticed that nothing rules out the two sides merging into a shared segment before they reach C. And nothing shows that the figure lies flat in a plane.
primer.quote: It is surprising that such a short, clear, and understandable proof can be so full of holes.

primer.heading: Why it matters
primer.body: The gaps do not mean the triangle fails to exist on paper. They mean Euclid's written assumptions are not enough to prove it. Extra postulates are needed. One example is a rule that two circles cross when their radii add up to more than the distance between their centres. Another is a rule that two straight lines meet at most once. This is a lesson about what a proof really requires: a picture can quietly supply facts that the stated rules never do.
primer.quote: There are models of geometry in which the circles do not intersect.

concepts.title: A circle keeps every point the same distance away
concepts.idea: Every point on a circle is exactly one radius from its centre, so a circle through B centred at A puts every point at distance AB from A.

predict.question: Draw the circle centred at A that passes through B. Now take a point D that sits strictly inside that circle, not on the curve itself. How does the distance from A to D compare with AB?
options: It depends on which direction D lies from A
why: Correct. Only points on the curve are exactly AB from A. Moving inward from the curve toward A brings a point closer, so D is less than AB away.

This is tempting because every point we moved was exactly AB away. But that held only because P stayed on the curve. Equal distance is what defines the curve, so a point off it cannot be exactly AB away.
You might picture 'inside' as 'further in'. But the inside of a circle is the side nearer the centre A. Points more than AB from A lie outside the circle, not inside.
Direction made no difference in the model: turning P never changed its distance. Every direction behaves the same. Inside means closer than AB, whichever way you go.

terms.means: The fixed point a circle is drawn around; every point of the circle is the same distance from it
That shared distance from the centre to any point on the circle; here it is the length AB

model.title: A point travelling around a ring drawn from A through B
model.note: Teaching model: a flat grid with A fixed in the middle and B always placed straight to the right of A. The ring is drawn exactly. All lengths are illustrative; the paper gives no numbers.

controls.label: Turn point P around the ring

steps.say: Here are two points: A in the middle, and B off to its right.
This slider sets how long AB is. The ring is drawn around A and always passes through B, so it grows as AB grows.
This slider swings point P around the ring, like the hand of a clock.
This box shows how far P is from A. Keep an eye on it.
Q is a fixed point you will use later.

explore.prompt: Now put what you've seen to work. You control the ring's size and P's position.

goals.text: Make the ring pass exactly through the fixed point Q.
hints: The ring goes through Q only if Q is exactly as far from A as every point on the ring.
Turning P won't help. Only the length of AB changes the ring's size.
Count grid squares: Q is 3 across and 4 up from A. How long is the straight line from A to Q?

goals.text: Now park P right on top of Q, so the gap between them almost vanishes.
hints: P can only reach Q if the ring passes through Q, so get that right first.
Once the ring goes through Q, turn P and watch the gap from P to Q shrink.
Seen from A, Q lies a little more than halfway between pointing right and pointing straight up.

feedback.correct: Right. A circle centred at A through B is exactly the set of points at distance AB from A. A point inside it is nearer to A than that, whichever direction it lies in.
feedback.incorrect: The equal distance belonged only to points on the curve, not to every point near it. Being exactly AB from A is what puts a point on the circle. Inside the circle means closer to A than AB, in any direction.

steps.say: Start with P sitting right on B. The distance from P to A is 3, the same as the length of AB.
Swing P a quarter turn, so it points straight up from A. The distance is still 3.
Swing it further round, past the bottom-left. Still 3. Turning P never changes how far it is from A.
That is what makes this ring a circle. A is its centre, and the fixed distance is its radius. Every point on a circle is one radius from the centre.
Now shrink AB to 2. The whole circle shrinks, and P's distance drops to 2 with it. The radius is simply the length of AB.
Stretch AB to 4 and park P up at the top left. AP and AB are now two different lines with exactly the same length, and nothing was measured.
This is Euclid's first move. Draw the circle centred at A through B, and any point that later turns up on it is guaranteed to be AB from A.

understand.explanation: A circle is drawn around a fixed centre, and every point on it lies the same distance from that centre: the radius. If you draw the circle centred at A so that it passes through B, the radius is the length AB. So any point on that circle is exactly AB from A, wherever on the curve it sits. Euclid's first proof leans on exactly this. He draws a circle around A through B and another around B through A, then takes a point C on the first circle and concludes that AC equals AB. The marginal note I.Def.15 marks this step as resting on the definition of a circle, not on any measurement.
understand.quote: Now, since the point A is the center of the circle CDB, therefore AC equals AB. Again, since the point B is the center of the circle CAE, therefore BC equals BA.

connect.caption: The paper states this in words, not as a formula, so this is the model's rule. P sits at angle θ (the turning slider) on a circle of radius r (the length of AB). Because cos²θ + sin²θ = 1, the distance AP always comes out to r, whatever θ is. This is the paper's 'AC equals AB', with C playing the part of P.

concepts.recap: On the circle centred at A through B, every point is exactly AB from A, so any point found on it inherits that length for free.

concepts.title: Where two circles cross, three sides match
concepts.idea: A point on both circles is distance AB from A and from B, so joining it to A and B gives three equal sides.

predict.question: Change the recipe. Keep the circle centred on A through B, but draw the circle around B with a radius only half as long as AB. The two circles still cross. If you join a crossing point C to A and B, what do you get?
options: A triangle with three equal sides, because any crossing point works
Two sides equal to AB and one side half as long
Nothing, because these circles cannot meet
Three equal sides, but only at the crossing above the line
why: Tempting if you remember 'take the crossing point' as the whole recipe. But a crossing only copies the radii it sits on. C is on the smaller circle, so BC is half of AB, not AB.
Right. C is on the circle around A, so AC = AB. C is on the half-size circle around B, so BC = half of AB. Two sides match and one is shorter, so the sides are not all equal.

The question says they still cross, and they do here: one circle has radius AB, the other half of AB, and their centres are AB apart. The trouble is not whether they meet but what length the crossing copies.
Above or below makes no difference. The two crossings are mirror images, and both sit on a circle of radius half of AB around B, so BC is the short side either way.

terms.means: A triangle whose three sides all have the same length
A step-by-step drawing recipe, here using only a straightedge and circles, that produces the required figure for any given starting line

model.title: Two rings: one centred on A, one centred on B
model.note: Teaching model: a flat grid with A fixed in the middle and B always straight to the right of A. Both rings have radius AB and are drawn exactly. The match readout allows a tiny tolerance because the turn slider moves in whole degrees. All lengths are illustrative; the paper gives no numbers.

controls.label: Turn point P around the ring

outputs.label: Distance from P to B
outputs.expr: sqrt((r * cos(theta * pi / 180) - r)^2 + (r * sin(theta * pi / 180))^2)

steps.say: This is the same picture as before: a ring centred on A that passes through B, and a point P that you move around it with the turn slider.
Here is what's new: a second ring, the same size, centred on B. It passes straight through A.
There is also a new line from B to P, and a readout of how far P is from B. Keep an eye on it.

explore.prompt: The two rings cross in more than one place. You've seen the crossing above AB. Go hunting for another spot where all three sides match.

goals.text: Find a spot below the line AB where P is as far from B as AB is long, so all three sides match
hints: P has to sit on both rings at once. Where else does the ring around B cut the ring around A?
The whole picture is a mirror image across the line AB. Look for the reflection of the crossing you already found.
Turn P past halfway round and keep going. Watch the distance to B fall back toward AB as P nears the lower crossing.

feedback.correct: Yes. A crossing point copies the radius of each circle it sits on. With the circle around B shrunk to half of AB, C is still AB from A but only half of AB from B. Only when both radii equal AB do all three sides match.
feedback.incorrect: A crossing point is not equal-sided by magic. It is equal-sided because it lies on two circles whose radii both equal AB. Change one radius and the side it controls changes with it: here BC becomes half of AB, so only two sides match.

steps.say: Start with P sitting right on top of B. Its distance to A is AB, but its distance to B is zero. One side matches and one doesn't.
Turn P partway up the ring. The distance to A doesn't budge, because P is still on the ring around A. The distance to B grows, but it's still short of AB.
Keep turning until P reaches the second ring. Now P is on both rings at once, so its distance to B is exactly AB too.
Compare the three readouts: AB, AP and BP are all the same. Euclid calls this crossing point C. A triangle with three equal sides is called an equilateral triangle.
Go past the crossing and P leaves the second ring. The distance to B now overshoots AB. Only the crossing gives three equal sides.
Now make AB longer and put P back at the crossing. Both rings grow together, and the three sides still match. A recipe that works for any starting line is called a construction.
Here is why it works. Being on the ring around A makes AC equal AB. Being on the ring around B makes BC equal AB. Two things equal to the same thing are equal to each other, so all three sides match.

understand.explanation: On the ring around A, P is always one AB away from A. Only where P also sits on the ring around B is it one AB away from B as well. At that crossing, which Euclid calls C, both new sides equal AB, so they equal each other and the triangle has three equal sides. Euclid's proof does exactly this. He draws a circle centred on A through B and another centred on B through A, joins a crossing point C to A and B, and uses the definition of a circle to argue that AC and BC each equal AB. The circles cross twice, above and below AB, and the paper's guide notes that either point will do. Like Euclid, this lesson simply takes for granted that the circles cross. Whether that is justified is a question for later.
understand.quote: Now, since the point A is the center of the circle CDB, therefore AC equals AB. Again, since the point B is the center of the circle CAE, therefore BC equals BA.

connect.caption: This is Euclid's chain of equalities from the proof, written in one line. AC is the 'distance from P to A' readout, which always equals AB because P rides the ring around A. BC is the 'distance from P to B' readout, which equals AB only at a crossing. AB is the length slider. When P sits at C, all three are equal.

concepts.recap: A point on both circles is one AB from A and one AB from B, so joining it to A and B closes a triangle with three equal sides, from either crossing point.

concepts.title: Every step must point to a stated rule
concepts.idea: Each line of Euclid's proof is licensed by a postulate, definition or common notion, and a step with no such licence is a gap.

terms.means: A basic rule accepted without proof, often a permission to draw something, such as a circle or a line
A statement of what a word means, such as what counts as a circle or an equilateral triangle
A general truth about equality that holds in any subject, such as 'things equal to the same thing are equal to one another'
A step in a proof that is stated without a rule to justify it

concepts.recap: In a proof, every claim needs a named rule behind it. A claim with none, like the existence of the point C, is a gap.

understand.explanation: A proof is a chain of steps, and each step should rest on a reason the reader has already accepted. One kind of reason is a postulate, a basic permission such as 'you may draw a circle with any centre and radius'. Another is a definition, which says what a word means, such as what a circle is. A third is a common notion, a general truth such as 'things equal to the same thing are equal to one another'. Results proved earlier can also serve. Editors print a short tag beside each step, such as Post.3 or C.N.1, to point to its reason. These tags are a reader's guide added by tradition, not part of Euclid's own text. When no rule licenses a step, critics call it a gap: the claim may well be true, but the proof has not earned it.
understand.quote: The abbreviations in the right column refer to postulates, definitions, common notions, and previously proved propositions. Each indicates a justification of a construction or conclusion in a sentence to its left.
understand.quote_where: Guide, 'Marginal references to postulates, definitions, etc.'

activities.title: Proposition 1, step by step, with the tag printed beside each step

steps.text: We are given a finite straight line AB. The task is to build an equilateral triangle on it.
steps.result: No rule is needed: this is what we are handed.

steps.text: Draw the circle with centre A through B. Then draw the circle with centre B through A.
steps.result: Tag: Post.3, the postulate that a circle may be drawn with any centre and any radius.

steps.text: From the point C at which the circles cut one another, join the straight lines CA and CB.
steps.result: Tag: Post.1, the postulate that a straight line may be drawn from one point to another.

steps.text: A is the centre of the circle through B and C, so AC equals AB. In the same way, B is the centre of the other circle, so BC equals BA.
steps.result: Tag: Def.15, the definition of a circle: every straight line from the centre to the circle is equal.

steps.text: AC and BC each equal AB, so AC equals BC.
steps.result: Tag: C.N.1, a common notion quoted in full in the text: 'things which equal the same thing also equal one another.'

steps.text: All three sides AC, AB and BC are equal, so triangle ABC is equilateral. The proof ends with Q.E.F., Latin for 'which was to be done'.
steps.result: Tag: Def.20, the definition of an equilateral triangle as one with three equal sides.

activities.takeaway: Every step names its permission. To check a proof, ask of each claim: which rule lets me say exactly this? The tags here are standard short summaries of Euclid's rules. The text itself quotes only C.N.1 in full.

activities.prompt: Match each step of the proof to the rule that licenses it.

pairs.text: Draw the circle centred at A through B, and the circle centred at B through A
pairs.target: Post.3: a circle may be drawn with any centre and radius
pairs.feedback: Drawing a circle is a construction, so it needs a permission. Post.3 grants it for any centre and any radius.

pairs.text: Join the straight lines CA and CB
pairs.target: Post.1: a straight line may be drawn between two points
pairs.feedback: Drawing a segment between two points is exactly what Post.1 allows.

pairs.text: AC equals AB, because A is the centre of the circle through B and C
pairs.target: Def.15: all lines from a circle's centre to the circle are equal
pairs.feedback: This is what being a circle means. C and B both lie on the circle around A, so their distances from A match.

pairs.text: AC and BC each equal AB, so AC equals BC
pairs.target: C.N.1: things equal to the same thing are equal to one another
pairs.feedback: This is not about circles at all. It is a general truth about equality, which is why it counts as a common notion.

pairs.text: Three equal sides, so triangle ABC is equilateral
pairs.target: Def.20: an equilateral triangle has three equal sides
pairs.feedback: Calling the triangle equilateral just applies the word's definition to the three equal sides already shown.

activities.takeaway: Constructions lean on a postulate. Facts about what shapes are lean on a definition. General reasoning about equality leans on a common notion.

activities.question: Read the joining step again: 'From the point C at which the circles cut one another, join CA and CB.' Its tag is Post.1, which lets you draw a line between two points you already have. Which claim in the proof has no rule behind it?

options.text: That we may draw the two circles
options.feedback: This one is covered. Post.3 allows a circle with any centre and radius, so both circles are licensed.

options.text: That there is a point C where the two circles cut one another
options.feedback: Right. Post.1 only lets you join points that already exist. No listed rule says the circles must meet. The text says plainly that 'there is no justification for its existence.' The step quietly assumes C, and a later concept looks at what rule would be needed.
This one is covered. It follows from C.N.1, because AC and BC each equal AB.

options.text: That a triangle with three equal sides is equilateral
options.feedback: This one is covered. Def.20 defines an equilateral triangle as one with three equal sides.

hints: For each claim, ask which rule from the match lets you say it.
Post.1 lets you join two points. Does any rule say where those points come from?
Look for something the proof uses without ever being given permission to have it.

concepts.title: Zeno's trap: what if the sides merge early?
concepts.idea: If the lines from A and B met at some point E and then shared a segment up to C, the enclosed triangle ABE would not be equilateral, so the proof needs lines to meet at most once.

predict.question: The paper's author warns that the sides from A and B might also cross each other several times on the way up, enclosing a chain of little regions like a necklace of bubbles. Which single added rule would rule out both that necklace and Zeno's merge?
options: Two straight lines cannot share a segment
Two straight lines can meet in at most one point
All radii of a circle are equal
Things equal to the same thing are equal to one another
why: Tempting, because this is the assumption Zeno himself said was needed. It blocks the merge. But lines that cross again and again without ever running together share no segment, so the necklace slips through.

Right. If two straight lines can meet only once, they can't meet at E and again at C, and they can't cross repeatedly. Every bad picture is ruled out at once. The paper says exactly this needs to be shown or assumed.
The proof already uses this, from the definition of a circle, to get AC = AB and BC = AB. Zeno's picture keeps those facts and still breaks the conclusion, so this rule can't be the fix.
The proof already uses this common notion to get AC = BC. It says nothing about how often lines meet, so it can't rule out either the merge or the necklace.

terms.means: A stretch of line that two lines share, running together side by side
A triangle with two equal sides, not necessarily all three
A case that fits every step of an argument yet makes its conclusion false

model.title: Lines from A and B that meet early at E and run together up to C
model.note: Teaching model: a flat sketch with AB = 4 units. In ordinary flat geometry the path A → E → C is bent, not straight. The picture shows the world Zeno imagined, where two 'straight' lines may run together after they meet, something Euclid's stated rules never forbid. Side lengths are measured as drawn. Numbers are illustrative, not from the paper.

controls.label: Where the lines first meet (0 = base, 1 = at C)
Show the straight lines AC and BC

outputs.label: AE as a share of AB

steps.say: Here is AB with the two circles from before, and C, the point where they cross.
Point E marks where the lines from A and B first meet. Right now it sits on C.
This slider slides E down from C toward the base.
These boxes measure the sides of the shaded region and the stretch from E up to C.
This switch draws the lines from A and B straight to C, for comparison.

explore.prompt: Slide the meeting point and watch how far the shaded region drifts from being equilateral, even though AE and BE always stay equal.

goals.text: Make the slanted sides of ABE shorter than three quarters of AB
hints: Which point decides how long AE and BE are?
The lower E sits, the shorter AE and BE get. Watch the 'AE as a share of AB' box.
You need to bring E a little under two thirds of the way up toward C.

goals.text: Shape ABE so its corner at E is a right angle, within 5°
hints: A tall, thin triangle has a sharp tip. A squat one has a wide tip.
With E at C the tip is 60°. Lower E to open the angle up, and watch the 'Angle at E' box.
The right angle arrives somewhere between halfway up and two thirds of the way up.

feedback.correct: Yes. Zeno's own fix, no shared segments, stops the merge but not lines that cross again and again. Only 'two straight lines meet at most once' closes every gap.
feedback.incorrect: The rules already in the proof (equal radii, equals of the same thing) stay true in Zeno's picture, and 'no shared segment' still allows repeated crossings. The paper says what's needed is that two straight lines meet in at most one point.

steps.say: Start with the honest case. E sits on C, there is no shared stretch, and AE equals AB: all three sides match.
Now suppose the lines from A and B meet early, at E, and then run together up to C. That shared stretch is called a common segment.
Look at the region they enclose: ABE. AE and BE still equal each other, because the picture is symmetric. A triangle with two equal sides is called isosceles.
But two equal sides aren't three. Pull E lower and AE shrinks well below AB.
Here is the trap. Each line still reaches C, on both circles, so the proof's claims 'AC equals AB' and 'BC equals AB' still read as true. Yet the figure they bound is ABE, not ABC.
On flat paper the path A to E to C is bent. Zeno's point is that nothing Euclid wrote down forbids two straight lines from merging like this.
Push E low and ABE turns squat, with a wide angle at E. Every step of the proof went through, but the result isn't equilateral. That makes it a counterexample.
Only when E sits exactly on C do the three sides match. To rule out the trap, the proof needs a rule about how often straight lines can meet.

understand.explanation: Euclid's proof shows AC = AB and BC = AB, then calls ABC equilateral. It never shows that the lines from A and B stay apart until they reach C. If they met early at E and shared a segment up to C, the region they enclose would be ABE. That region has two equal sides, AE and BE, but both are shorter than AB, so it is isosceles, not equilateral. Proclus reports this critique from Zeno of Sidon. Zeno saw that blocking it requires assuming straight lines cannot share a segment. The paper's author judges the critique sound and the old attempted refutations faulty, because they leaned on properties of lines that Euclid never proved or stated.
understand.quote: Zeno of Sidon criticized the proof because it was not shown that the sides do not meet before they reach the vertices. Suppose AC and BC meet at E before they reach C, that is, the straight lines AEC and BEC have a common segment EC. Then they would contain a triangle ABE which is not equilateral, but isosceles.
understand.quote_where: Critiques of the proof: Why does ABC contain an equilateral triangle?

check.task: Put E where the shared stretch EC is longer than side AE, so most of each line is the merged part.
check.hint: The shared stretch grows as E drops, while AE shrinks toward half of AB. Go low.
check.misconception: That the merge can only be a tiny sliver near C, leaving a figure that is still essentially the equilateral triangle. In fact, nothing in Euclid's stated rules limits how early the lines merge, so the enclosed region can be far from equilateral.

connect.caption: The paper gives no equation here; this is the model's rule. E sits at height 2√3 × t above the middle of AB (slider t), so Pythagoras gives AE and BE. They always equal each other, but they equal AB only when t = 1, that is, when E is C.

concepts.recap: Equal radii prove AC = AB and BC = AB, but if the lines could merge early the enclosed figure would be isosceles, not equilateral, so the proof silently needs straight lines to meet at most once.

concepts.title: Nothing in Euclid's rules makes the circles cross
concepts.idea: Two circles cross only when their radii add up to more than the distance between their centres, and that fact is a postulate Euclid never stated, so the point C is assumed rather than proved.

predict.question: Try the same two-circle trick to build a triangle with sides 2, 3 and 6. Draw a base of length 6, a circle of radius 2 around one end and a circle of radius 3 around the other. Do the circles give you a crossing point for the top corner?
options: Yes: any two circles you can draw will cross somewhere
No: 2 + 3 is less than 6, so the circles miss each other
Only if you draw them carefully enough
Yes: Euclid's postulates let you draw any circle, so the crossing comes for free
why: Euclid's own picture makes crossing look automatic. But circles cross only when their radii add up to more than the distance between centres, and here they add to 5, short of 6.

Right. The radii total 5, less than the distance of 6, so the circles never reach each other. The paper notes the same kind of postulate is needed in Proposition I.22, which also builds a triangle from circles.
Care cannot help here. The gap comes from the lengths themselves: radii of 2 and 3 cannot span a distance of 6, however precisely you draw.
Being allowed to draw a circle is not the same as being promised that two circles meet. That promise is the missing postulate, and here it would be false anyway, because 2 + 3 < 6.

terms.means: Two circles that touch at exactly one point without crossing
A world of points, lines and circles that obeys a chosen set of rules; some obey all of Euclid's stated rules yet have circles that never meet

model.title: Two circles, and the point where they cross (if they do)
model.note: Teaching model: A and B sit on a flat, gap-free plane, and C is computed with modern coordinates. Circles also fail to cross when one sits wholly inside the other; the model checks that too. Numbers are illustrative, not from the paper.

points.y: (r1 + r2 > dist && abs(r1 - r2) < dist) ? sqrt(max(0, r1*r1 - pow((dist*dist + r1*r1 - r2*r2) / (2*dist), 2))) : 30
points.label: C

steps.say: Here are two circles: one drawn around point A, one drawn around point B.
This slider sets how big the circle around A is.
This one sets the circle around B.
And this one slides B nearer to A or farther away.
Point C marks where the circles cross, if they cross at all. These boxes track the radii added together and whether a crossing exists.

explore.prompt: Now you try. Make the crossing point C vanish, then make it come back in a harder setting.

goals.text: Without moving A and B, shrink the circles until they no longer cross.
hints: What has to happen to the two radii added together?
Watch the 'Radii added together' box and compare it with the distance from A to B.
Keep shrinking the radii until their total drops below the distance, not just equal to it.

goals.text: Get the circles to cross even though B is more than 6.5 away from A.
hints: If A and B are far apart, what must be true of the radii for the circles to reach each other?
With the starting radii, the circles cannot span that distance. Both circles need to grow.
Move B out past the target first, then grow both radii until point C reappears and the margin box turns positive.

feedback.correct: Yes. The radii add to 5, less than the distance of 6, so the circles never meet and there is no top corner. The lengths have to allow a crossing; drawing the circles does not guarantee one.
feedback.incorrect: It is easy to assume two drawn circles always cross, because Euclid's picture always shows it. But circles cross only when their radii add up to more than the distance between centres. Here 2 + 3 = 5 is less than 6, so they miss.

steps.say: Start with Euclid's picture. Both circles have radius equal to AB, and C sits where they cross.
Shrink both circles a little. The radii now add to 4, still more than the distance of 3, so they still cross.
Shrink them until the radii add to exactly 3, the distance. The circles touch at one point on AB; circles touching like this are called tangent. Nothing sits above the line, so C has gone.
Shrink a bit more and a gap opens. There is no crossing point at all.
Size is not the only thing that matters. Give the circles back radius 3, then pull B out to 6.5. The radii total 6, short of 6.5, and again there is no C.
So here is the rule: two circles cross only when their radii add up to more than the distance between their centres.
In Euclid's setup both radii equal AB, so they add to twice AB, which is always more than AB. Whatever the length, every drawing shows a crossing.

But a drawing is not a proof. No Euclid postulate says these circles must meet. The paper notes a model of geometry can follow his stated rules yet have circles that never meet. So C is simply assumed.

understand.explanation: Two circles cross only when their radii add up to more than the distance between their centres. There is also a smaller extra condition: neither circle can sit wholly inside the other. In Euclid's construction both radii equal AB, so they add to twice AB, and every drawing shows a crossing. Yet the proof just names C as the point where the circles cut one another, and it never cites a rule that guarantees it. The paper points out that no Euclid postulate here says such a point exists, and that a postulate like the sum-of-radii rule is needed. It adds that there is a model of geometry in which the circles do not intersect, so the first proof of the Elements assumes C rather than proving it.
understand.quote: Indeed, some postulate is needed for that conclusion, such as “If the sum of the radii of two circles is greater than the line joining their centers, then the two circles intersect.”
understand.quote_where: Critiques of the proof: Why does the point C exist?

check.task: Put the circles exactly on the boundary between crossing and missing: touching each other from outside at a single point.
check.hint: The boundary is where the radii added together exactly equal the distance from A to B. Watch the margin box.
check.misconception: That circles either clearly overlap or clearly miss, with no exact tipping point set by the radii and the distance between centres.

connect.caption: The paper states this rule in words, as a postulate Euclid would need. Here it is written as an inequality: the radius around A plus the radius around B must exceed the distance AB. When the inequality holds and neither circle lies inside the other, the crossing output reads 1. In Euclid's case r_{A} = r_{B} = AB, so the left side is 2·AB, which beats AB. The inequality holds every time, but no stated postulate turns that into a guaranteed point C.

concepts.recap: Circles cross only when their radii add up to more than the distance between centres. Euclid's first proof relies on that crossing, but none of his stated rules guarantees it.
